The Section on Conduct:
The Conduct of the Four Castes. Now, therefore, on the peak of the Snowy Mountain, in the abode of the Devadāru forest—
In ancient times, the sages questioned Vyāsa as he sat with his mind one-pointedly concentrated.
O son of Satyavatī, please describe in due order the dharma that is beneficial for human beings in the current Kali age, as well as the rules of purification and conduct.
Having heard those words of the sage, Aṅga— who resembled the sun, possessed great splendor, and was well-versed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis— replied together with his disciples.
"I am not an omniscient knower of all truths; how then could I speak on Dharma? My father alone should be questioned," so Vyāsa spoke to his son.
Then all those sages, desiring to know the true meaning of the principles of dharma,
placed the sage Vyāsa at their head and went to the Badarikā hermitage.
It was strewn with various flowering creepers, adorned with fruit-bearing trees,
endowed with rivers and springs, and beautified by sacred bathing places.
Abounding with the cries of wild beasts and birds, surrounded by the abodes of deities,
and adorned with the dances and songs of yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas.
In the midst of that assembly of sages, the one of great splendor saw Parāśara, the son of Śakti, seated comfortably and surrounded by a multitude of eminent sages.
Having joined his palms in the gesture of reverence, Vyāsa, together with the sages,
honored him with circumambulations, salutations, and hymns of praise.
Then, with a heart full of contentment, the great sage Parāśara, that bull among munis, sat down and said, "Welcome; speak."
Having said, "It is well; it is right," Vyāsa immediately asked:
"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, if you know [this], out of love for me or because of my devotion."
"O father, tell me the Dharma; for I am worthy of your favor.
I have heard the Dharmas of Manu, as well as those of Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa."
The Gārgya, the Gautama, and likewise those recorded by Uśanas; those of Atri, Viṣṇu, Saṃvarta, Dakṣa, and likewise Aṅgiras.
From Śātātapa and Hārīta, and likewise from Yājñavalkya;
the laws composed by Āpastamba, as well as those of Śaṅkha and Likhita.
The works composed by Kātyāyana, as well as those of the sage Prācetasa, have indeed been heard by me as they were spoken by you; the meanings of these scriptures are not forgotten.
In this Manvantara, throughout the ages beginning with Kṛta and Tretā,
all dharmas arise in the Kṛta age and all are lost in the Kali age.
Speak briefly on the common conduct of the four castes—
that which is to be practiced by those learned in dharma belonging to all four varṇas.
"O knower of the true nature of Dharma, speak at length concerning its subtle and gross aspects.
At the conclusion of Vyāsa’s words, Parāśara, the foremost of sages, [replied].
He has declared the determination of Dharma, both subtle and gross, in detail.
Listen, my son, I shall speak; let the sages likewise listen.
In every kalpa, through their destruction and origination, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Maheśvara are always the determiners of the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous.
No one is the author of the Veda; rather, the four-faced Brahmā remembers the Veda.
In the same way, Manu remembers the dharmas at the beginning of each successive kalpa.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind; in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages they are different;
and in the Kali age they are yet another, according to the nature of each respective age.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so.
In the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; in the Kali age, charity alone.
In the Kṛta age, the laws of Manu were established; in the Tretā, those of Gautama are remembered;
in the Dvāpara, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, the Smṛti of Parāśara is recorded.
In the Kṛta age one should abandon the country; in the Tretā age, one should leave the village;
in the Dvāpara age, the single family; but in the Kali age, one should abandon the doer alone.
In the Kṛta age, one falls by mere conversation; in the Tretā, by touching [the food];
in the Dvāpara, by taking the food; but in the Kali age, one falls by the performance of the act itself.
In the Kṛta age, a curse takes effect immediately; in the Tretā, after ten days;
in the Dvāpara, after one month; but in the Kali age, after one year.
In the Kṛta age, giving is performed after approaching [the recipient]; in the Tretā, it is given after calling out;
in the Dvāpara, it is given to one who asks; and in the Kali age, it is given through service.
Giving after approaching the recipient is the highest; giving only after calling out to him is middling;
giving to one who asks is lowest; but giving to a servant is fruitless.
In the Kali age, dharma is indeed conquered by adharma, and truth by falsehood;
kings are overcome by thieves, and men by women.
The Agnihotra sacrifices fall into ruin, reverence for gurus perishes,
and maidens give birth [to children] constantly in this Kali Yuga.

In the Kṛta age, however, the vital breaths reside in the bones; in the Tretā, they are supported by the flesh; in the Dvāpara, they are in the blood; but in the Kali age, they are situated in food and other such things.

One must not engage in the censure of those who are the preservers of dharma in age after age, nor of those twice-born ones who exist in various places; for such twice-born ones are indeed the very forms of the ages.
In every age, however, the remaining capacity [for penance] has been described by the Sage;
and that which was spoken by Parāśara is also prescribed as the expiation.
"Having recollected all of that this very day, I speak it to you. O preeminent sages, listen to the conduct of the four castes."
The meritorious and purifying doctrine of Parāśara, which destroys evil,
was conceived for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas and for the establishment of Dharma.
The conduct of all four castes is the protector of dharma;
for those whose bodies have fallen away from right conduct, dharma becomes turned away from them.
A Brāhmaṇa who is constantly devoted to the six duties, who honors the deities and guests, and who eats only the remnants of the oblation, does not come to ruin.
Bathing at the twilights, silent recitation, burnt offerings, worship of the deities and guests,
hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice— these are the six duties to be performed day after day.
Whether he be beloved or hated, a fool or even a scholar— whosoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is a guest who brings about the attainment of heaven.

One should recognize as a guest (atithi) one who has come from a long journey, one who is weary, and one who has arrived for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; a guest is not one who arrives beforehand.
One should never accept as a guest someone who belongs to the same village;
because he has arrived without a fixed time, he is therefore called an *atithi* (guest).
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other such courtesies,
by offering the respectful water (arghya), a seat, and by washing his feet.
With faith, by the gift of food, by pleasant inquiries and replies,
and by following one who is departing, the householder should generate affection.
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
the ancestors of that person do not eat for fifteen years.
For one whose guest departs with unfulfilled hopes, even if he has offered a thousand loads of wood and a hundred jars of clarified butter, his burnt offering is as good as useless.
One should sow seed in a good field and bestow wealth upon a worthy recipient;
for what is sown in a good field and given to a worthy recipient does not perish.
One should not inquire about [another's] lineage (*gotra*), religious school (*caraṇa*), Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), or sacred learning (*śruta*).
One should conceive of the Divine within the heart, for He is composed of all the gods.
A Brahmin who is a performer of excellent vows is indeed unprecedented, just as one who is a guest of honor is unprecedented;
those two, constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas, are unprecedented day after day.
When the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has commenced and a mendicant has arrived at the house,
one should set aside food for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva and then dismiss the mendicant.
Both the ascetic and the student are masters of cooked food.
Having eaten without first giving food to these two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A wandering mendicant (parivrāj) should give three morsels of alms to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin);
thereafter, if he has the means, he may give as much as desired, provided it is not forbidden.
One should offer water in the hand of the ascetic, and again offer water after giving alms;
that alms-food is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is comparable to the ocean.
He whose umbrella, horse, and elephant are indeed prosperous,
and who occupies the station of Indra— that man one should not question.
A mendicant is capable of removing the sin committed by the community (vaiśvadeva),
but the community cannot remove the faults committed by the mendicant.
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite—
know that all of them are fruitless and fall into an impure hell.
Those who are excluded from the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and cast out from the guest-offering (ātithya),
they all go to hell and enter the womb of a crow.
Even if he is a sinner, an outcaste, a slayer of Brahmins, or a murderer of his father,
when he arrives during the Vaiśvadeva rite, he is a guest who leads one to heaven.
He who eats with his head wrapped, he who eats facing south,
or he who places his hand upon his left foot— verily, the Rākṣasas eat that food.
The king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms while remaining without vows and unlearned in the Vedas; for such a village provides sustenance to thieves.
For a Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapons in hand and wielding the rod of punishment,
should conquer the enemy armies and protect the earth in accordance with Dharma.
One should pluck flower after flower, but one should not cause the destruction of the roots; like a garland-maker in a garden, and not like a charcoal-burner.
Acquiring property, as well as gems, the protection of cattle,
agriculture, and trade— this is declared to be the livelihood of a Vaiśya. For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is said to be the highest duty.
If one performs anything otherwise [than prescribed], that shall be fruitless for him.
Salt, honey, oil, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk—these do not cause defilement for those of the Śūdra caste; one may sell them among all [classes].
By selling meat from the middle of an animal, by eating that which is forbidden to eat,
and by having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, a Śūdra falls from his status at that very moment.
By drinking the milk of a tawny cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman,
and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Veda, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Cāṇḍāla. Hereafter [is described] the ritual conduct of the householder in the Kali age.
One should, according to one's ability, promote the common dharma that has come down through the four castes and the stages of life.
I shall proclaim that [dharma] first, according to the words of Parāśara:
a Brahmin, while engaged in the six duties, may also perform the work of agriculture.
One should not yoke an ox that is hungry, thirsty, or exhausted.
A Brahmin should not drive an ox that is deficient in limb, diseased, or impotent.
One should cause a bull that has firm limbs, is well-fed, is pleasant to hear, and is free from impotence, to work for half the day; thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath.
One should practice the recitation of prayers, the worship of the gods, burnt offerings, and Vedic study in this manner.
A twice-born man should feed one, two, three, or four *snātaka* Brahmins.
Likewise, [he may perform these acts] with grains earned by himself on a field ploughed by himself.
One should perform the five sacrifices and cause the initiation for a Vedic sacrifice to be undertaken.
One who sells sesame seeds or liquids is equal to one who sells grain;
such is the livelihood of a Brahmin, as is the selling of grass, wood, and the like.
If a Brāhmaṇa should engage in agriculture, he incurs a great fault;
the sin that a fisherman incurs in a single year, he incurs by that [act].
One who ploughs with an iron-tipped wooden pole for a single day [becomes a *lāṅgalin*];
likewise, one who uses a noose, a fisherman, a hunter, and a fowler [are all equal].
The non-giver and the cultivator alike—all these share equally [in the merit].
Having cut down trees, having broken the earth, and having killed worms and insects;
A farmer is liberated from all sins by means of the *khala-yajña* (the sacrifice at the threshing floor),
provided that he does not fail to give to the twice-born when he has arrived at the root of his harvest.
He is a thief, he is most wicked; one should designate him as a slayer of a Brahmin.
Having given a sixth part to the king and a twenty-first part to the gods, [he may be purified].
By giving a thirtieth part of [the merit] to Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins.
A Kṣatriya, too, having engaged in agriculture, should worship the gods and the Brahmins.
A Vaiśya and likewise a Śūdra should practice agriculture, trade, and the arts.
Those Śūdras who, having abandoned service to the twice-born, perform improper work [are censured].
They indeed become short-lived and undoubtedly go to hell.
This is the eternal dharma for all four castes as well.
Therefore, I shall now declare the purification regarding birth and likewise death:
Brāhmaṇas become pure after three days in the case of a death or a birth.
A Kṣatriya becomes pure in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days,
and a Śūdra becomes pure in a month, according to the word of Parāśara.
In the case of attending upon Brahmins, O dear one, purification of the limbs occurs;
however, in the case of the birth of Brahmins or contact with a deity, it is ordained [that the entire body be purified].
In the case of a birth-impurity, a Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in one month.
A Brahmin who is endowed with both the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day; one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days, while one devoid of both is purified in ten days.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from his birth-rites and actions, who is devoid of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyopāsana),
and who merely bears the name of a Brahmin, shall remain impure for ten days.
Heirs who share a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) but have separate wives and dwellings— among them,
the birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (vipatti) shall belong to that [specific family] alone.
That birth-impurity (sūtaka) remains within the lineage until the fourth generation;
however, at the fifth generation—or rather, one born in the fifth degree of one's own family line—one attains the cessation of inheritance.
In the fourth [generation], there shall be a ten-night period; in the case of a male in the fifth, six nights.
In the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days.
In the case of death by fire or drowning, as well as death in a foreign land,
and when a child has died or one has renounced the world (saṃnyasta), immediate purification is ordained.

If it is heard that someone who belongs to one's own lineage has died in another country, one should not observe the three-night impurity; rather, by bathing for a single day and night, one becomes pure immediately.
If a Brahmin who has gone to another land meets with the destruction of his body due to exhaustion or the passage of time, and the lunar day [of his death] is not known;
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, and on whichever eleventh day is dark,
one should perform the offering of water, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and the śrāddha ceremony.
For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and for those who have just emerged from the womb,
there is no consecration by fire, no period of impurity, and no water libation.
If a fetus miscarries or is aborted from a woman,
the period of impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had remained in the womb.
Until the fourth month, it shall be called *srāva* (a miscarriage); in the fifth and sixth months, it is a *pāta* (a fall/miscarriage).
Beyond that, it is a birth (*prasūti*), and there shall be *sūtaka* (impurity due to childbirth) for ten days.
Upon the death of one whose teeth have not yet emerged, or who has recently emerged, or one for whom the tonsure ceremony has been performed,
or one who has passed away after the performance of the fire-rite (agnisaṃskaraṇa), there shall be impurity for three nights.

Until the birth of teeth, impurity is declared to be immediate; until the tonsure ceremony, it is known as *naiṣikī* (lasting one night); until the instruction for the vows (*vrata-ādeśa*), it lasts three nights; and beyond that, ten nights.
For those in whose house a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) resides, and in which the sacrificial fire is offered,
and who do not engage in [unlawful] contact, there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka).
A Brahmin becomes defiled through contact [with impure persons], as well as at birth and death;
however, for one who has withdrawn from such contact, there is neither impurity from a corpse nor impurity from childbirth.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female and male slaves,
barbers, kings, and those well-versed in the Vedas are proclaimed to be pure immediately.

A twice-born man who observes his vows, one purified by a sacrificial session (*satra*), and one who has maintained the sacred fires— there is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for these, nor for a king, nor for one whom the monarch desires [to be pure].
When a Brahmin who has been invited for a funeral rite, a sacrifice, or a gift is in distress,
the sages have prescribed that he becomes pure after the time required for the completion of that task.
But during childbirth, if there is no confusion of castes, the householder should not perform the Gṛhamedhī sacrifice;
the mother becomes pure after ten days by bathing, while the father is pure immediately.

For all [relatives], there is impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca); however, for the mother and father, there is birth-impurity (sūtaka). Birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution (upaspṛśya).
If a twice-born man has sexual intercourse with his wife while she is in childbirth,
he incurs the impurity of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity), even if he is a Brahmin learned in the six Vedāṅgas.
"Defilement arises from association; indeed, there is no other defilement for a twice-born man.
Therefore, a wise person should avoid association with every effort."
Pṣ 3.27ab: However, during marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, even if a death or birth impurity occurs in the interval, Pṣ 3.27cd:
material that was previously intended [for the rite] and is being given does not become defiled.
If death or birth occurs within ten days [of a previous impurity],
the Brāhmaṇa shall remain impure for as long as that [original period] has not yet expired.
For those who perish for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as for those killed during the seizure of prisoners or cattle,
and for those who perish in battles, there is impurity for one night.
"There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and one who is slain facing the enemy in battle."
Wherever a hero, surrounded by enemies, is slain,
he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not utter words of cowardice.
Upon seeing a Brahmin who has renounced all worldly ties (saṃnyasta), the sun moves from its place;
thinking, "He shall pierce my orb and proceed to the supreme abode."
But he who, when the armies are broken and fleeing in every direction,
goes forth as their protector, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
The daughters of the gods carry away that hero whose limbs are wounded by the cutting of arrows, mallets, and clubs, and they delight him.
Thousands of celestial nymphs run in haste toward the hero slain in battle, crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine!"
That which the Brahmins seeking heaven attain through hosts of sacrifices and through austerity,
the heroes go there in an instant by abandoning their lives in a noble battle.
By victory one obtains fortune; even by death, one gains celestial nymphs.
Since this body perishes in an instant, what anxiety can there be regarding death in battle?

When blood flows from the forehead of one in battle and enters his mouth, that is indeed said to be equal to drinking Soma; it is seen as such when performed according to the rules in the sacrifice of war.
Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in due succession.
For those who perform auspicious deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin;
for them, purification is ordained immediately upon immersion in water.

Having carried and cremated a deceased person who was neither a relative nor a friend, even if that person were the best of the twice-born, one becomes pure through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having followed a deceased kinsman or even a non-kinsman out of his own desire,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
If a Brāhmaṇa follows a deceased Kṣatriya out of ignorance,
he remains impure for one day and becomes purified by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Brāhmaṇa follows the corpse of a Vaiśya out of ignorance,
he shall observe impurity for two nights and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
If a Brahmin, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse as it is being carried out,
he shall remain impure for three nights.
When three nights have thus passed, he should go to a river that flows to the ocean;
by performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and consuming clarified butter, he becomes purified.
When a Śūdra has been cremated and has reached the edge of the water, the twice-born should then follow him; this is the eternal law. (Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa 3.47)
Whether out of excessive pride, excessive anger, affection, or even fear,
if a woman or a man should commit an abortion, this course of action is prescribed.
But one who is filled with pus and blood sinks into blinding darkness;
for sixty thousand years, he enters hell.
One should not cause impurity, nor [the offering of] water, nor fire, nor the shedding of tears;
likewise, the bearers, the givers of fire, and those who cut the bonds [are exempt].
"Prajāpati has declared that they are purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance:
[the meat] of one killed by cows, likewise of one who has hanged himself, and of one killed by a Brāhmaṇa."
Those Brahmins who touch [the corpse], those who carry it, those who provide the fire, others who follow as attendants, and those who cut the bonds; // Pṣ 4.5 //
Having been purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance, they should provide a meal for Brahmins and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.
For three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot milk;
for three days one should drink hot clarified butter; and for three days one should subsist on air alone.
One should drink six palas of water, then drink three palas of milk, and finally drink one pala of clarified butter; this is prescribed as the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
If a Brahmin should unintentionally associate with those who have fallen from their caste (patita) and others,
he shall observe [the penance] for five days, ten days, twelve days, or even more.
Whether for a month, half a month, one month, or even two months;
or for half a year, a year, or one year, and even beyond that, he remains equal to him.
In the first fortnight, one should observe the three-night fast; in the second, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance;
and in the third fortnight, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
In the fourth [case], it should be a ten-night penance; in the fifth, a parāka is prescribed.
In the sixth, one should perform a cāndrāyaṇa; but in the seventh, two aindavas.

For the sake of purification, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months even during the eighth [period]; the number of *suvarṇas* given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is determined by the number of fortnights.
But that woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband,
goes to hell when she dies, and becomes a widow again and again.
But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him, is joined with the terrible sin of foeticide; there is no doubt in this matter.
She who disregards her husband— whether he be poor, diseased, or foolish—
is born as a female dog after death, and again and again as a sow.
A woman who, while her husband is alive, observes a fast or performs a vow, takes away the lifespan of her husband; that woman shall go to hell.
"If a woman performs a vow without even having asked her husband, all of that shall go to the Rākṣasas; thus Manu has declared."
But she who behaves wickedly toward her kinsmen or those of her own caste,
or she who causes an abortion— one should never speak with her.
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a Brahmin, that sin is doubled in the destruction of an embryo. There can be no expiation for her; her abandonment is ordained.
Neither by the performance of domestic rites nor again by the Agnihotra sacrifice does one become pure;
he who has turned his back on Dharma becomes a Cāṇḍāla in his actions.
If seed brought by a flood or the wind sprouts in someone's field, that owner of the field receives the crop;
the owner of the seed does not deserve a share.
In the same manner, two types of sons born of another's wife are traditionally known as the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*.
The *kuṇḍa* is he who is born while the husband is still living; the *golaka* is he who is born when the husband is dead.
The legitimate son (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the adopted son (datta), and the son made (kṛtrima)—
whichever son the mother or the father may give away, he becomes an adopted son (dattaka).
The elder brother who remains unmarried while his younger brother marries, the younger brother who marries before his elder,
the woman through whom the marriage is contracted, the giver of the girl, and the officiating priest as the fifth— all these go to hell.
For the elder brother who marries before his younger brother, there are two *kṛcchra* penances; for the maiden, a single *kṛcchra*;
for the giver, a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*; and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) shall perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*.
There is no fault in marrying a hunchback, a dwarf, a eunuch, one who stammers, one who is mentally dull,
one blind from birth, one who is deaf, or one who is mute.
The son of a paternal uncle, the son of a co-wife, and likewise the son of another's wife—
there is no fault in superseding them for the purpose of uniting with a wife and maintaining the sacred fire.
When an elder brother is present, one should not perform the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*);
however, having obtained his permission, one may do so, according to the word of Śaṅkha.
When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.
That woman who, upon the death of her husband, remains steadfast in the vow of celibacy,
attains heaven when she dies, just like those lifelong students of sacred knowledge.
There are thirty-five million hairs on a human being;
for as long as that number of years shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
so too does a woman, having rescued her husband, rejoice together with him. However,
that best of the twice-born who has been bitten by wolves, dogs, jackals, or similar creatures—
Having bathed, he should mutter the Gāyatrī, the purifier, the mother of the Vedas.
Bathing with cow-horn water at the confluence of great rivers,
or even by beholding the ocean, one bitten by a dog shall become pure.
If a twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies, mastered the sciences, and performed his vows is bitten by a dog,
he becomes pure by bathing with water containing gold and consuming clarified butter.
But one who has been bitten by a dog while observing a vow should fast for three nights;
having drunk ghee and water infused with *kuśa* grass, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
Whether he be one who has failed in his vows or one who observes them, if a twice-born man is bitten by a dog,
he becomes purified by prostrating himself and being gazed upon by Brahmins with their eyes.
For that which has been smelled by a dog, licked by it, or scratched by its claws,
washing with water is prescribed, as well as heating with fire.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a wolf,
she becomes pure immediately upon seeing the risen planets or stars.
When the moon is never visible during the dark fortnight,
one should look toward whichever direction the moon is moving.
If the best of the twice-born is bitten by a dog in a village where no Brāhmaṇas reside,
he becomes pure immediately by circumambulating a bull and bathing.
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is struck by a Caṇḍāla, a dog-cooker, cattle, or other Brahmins; or if he dies having been killed by poison or by his own hand.
A Brahmin who performs the cremation for such a Brahmin without the recitation of mantras shall himself be burned in the world-fire.
This applies in every way to those who touch the corpse, carry it, cremate it, or are among the sapinda relatives.
Afterwards, at the instruction of the Brahmins, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having taken up the burnt bones once more, the twice-born man should wash them with milk.

One who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), being compelled by time while traveling abroad, should have his own fires rekindled separately and independently by his own fire. (Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra 5.13)
When his body has met its destruction, fire remains in his house;
O bulls among sages, listen now to the ritual for the consecration of the fire of a deceased person.
Having spread out a black antelope skin and fashioned a human figure with kuśa grass,
one should [place] six hundred and one stalks of palāśa wood.
One should place forty [beads] on the head, and one hundred should be placed on the neck;
one should place one hundred on the two arms, and exactly ten on the fingers.
One should apply one hundred [strokes] on the buttocks, and likewise two hundred on the abdomen;
one should apply eight on the testicles and place five on the penis.
One should assign twenty-one [parts] to the two thighs, two hundred to the knees and shanks, and six to the toes of the feet; thereafter, one should place the sacrificial vessel.
Having placed the *śamyā* upon the penis and the two *araṇis* upon the testicles,
one should place the *juhū* in the right hand and the *upabhṛt* in the left.
One should place a mortar upon the ears and set a pestle upon the back;
having cast a grindstone upon the chest, one should place rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds in the mouth.
One should place the *prokṣaṇī* water on the ear, and the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) on the two eyes;
one should place pieces of gold (*hiraṇyaśakala*) on the ears, the eyes, the mouth, and the nose.
One should deposit all the implements of the *agnihotra* there without exception.
With the words, "This [offering] is for the heavenly world, svāhā," one should offer a single oblation once.
The son, or a brother, or even another relative should provide [the materials];
the wise should perform the cremation rite exactly as prescribed.
One should perform such a rite as this; it is traditionally taught that [the performer] attains the world of Brahmā.
Those twice-born who cremate him likewise go to the supreme goal.
Driven by their own deluded intellects, they perform actions otherwise than prescribed;
such people indeed become short-lived and fall into an impure hell.
Hereafter, I shall declare the expiation for the killing of living beings.
It was previously spoken by Parāśara and expanded upon even regarding the meaning of Manu’s work.
For killing a curlew, a crane, a swan, a ruddy goose, a cock,
a web-footed bird, or a śarabha, one is purified in a day and night.
A crane, a lapwing, a parrot, a pigeon, a snake,
a crocodile, and a vulture are purified by fasting during the night.
One who kills a wolf, a crow, or a pigeon, or a śāri bird, a partridge, or a hawk,
becomes pure by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) both at dawn and at dusk while remaining within the water.
One who kills vultures, hawks, rabbits, dogs, or owls,
and one who eats uncooked food, shall stand for a day during the three periods of the day, subsisting only on air.
The *valguṇī*, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the *kokila*, the *khañjarīṭaka*, the *lāvika*,
and those with red wings— these are purified by eating only at night.
Having killed a kāraṇḍava or a cakora bird, a piṅgalā, or a kurara crane,
as well as one belonging to the lineage of Bhāradvāja and others, one becomes purified by worshipping Śiva.
Upon killing a bheruṇḍa, a cāṣa, a bhāsa, a pārāvata, or a kapiñjala,
as well as any other bird whatsoever, one must abstain from food for a day and a night.
Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a non-venomous serpent,
one should feed the Brahmins kṛsara (rice and sesame) and give an iron staff as the sacrificial fee.
Having killed a *śiśumāra* (crocodile), a monitor lizard, a tortoise, or a porcupine,
as well as one who eats the fruit of the eggplant, is purified after a day and a night.
One who kills a wolf, a jackal, a bear,
or a hyena should give a *prastha* measure of sesame seeds to a twice-born man and subsist on air for three days.
For the killing of an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, or a camel,
the penance is one day and night, along with immersion in water at the three junctions of the day.
By killing a deer, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger,
one is purified in three nights and by the satiation of Brahmins with water offerings.
A killer of deer, antelopes, or boars, or a killer of sheep or goats,
shall fast for a day and night and eat only food that has not been ploughed by the furrow.
In this manner, having stayed for a day and night among all these four-footed forest-dwelling creatures, he should stand and recite prayers to Jātavedas.
He who should kill an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman,
having performed two Prājāpatya penances, must give eleven bulls as a sacrificial fee.
If one should strike a Vaiśya or even a Kṣatriya who is free from fault,
he too shall perform two Kṛcchra penances and give twenty cows as a sacrificial fee.
Having killed a Vaiśya, a Śūdra attached to ritual acts, or a superior twice-born man engaged in improper work,
one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and give thirty cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
If someone has killed a Caṇḍāla near a Brāhmaṇa,
he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Whether it be by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even by another [lower caste],
when the death penalty for a Caṇḍāla has been incurred, one is purified by half of a Kṛcchra penance.
If a thief, a dog-cooker (outcaste), or a Caṇḍāla is struck down by a Brahmin,
he becomes pure after staying for one day and night and bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a thief, a dog-cooker (outcaste), or a Caṇḍāla are struck down by a Brāhmaṇa,
he becomes pure by staying for one day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one has slept together with Caṇḍālas, one should fast for three nights;
having traveled along a path used by a Caṇḍāla, one becomes pure by the recollection of the Gāyatrī.
Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should immediately look at the sun;
upon touching a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
If an elder brother drinks water from a well dug by a Caṇḍāla,
he becomes pure after fasting for one day and night, provided it was done unintentionally.
Having drunk water from a well that has been touched by a Caṇḍāla or a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
one attains purification after three nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel (yāvaka).
If a twice-born man drinks water contained in a jar belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he who spits it out immediately should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If one does not vomit the water [consumed] and it is digested within the body, the Prājāpatya penance should not be assigned; rather, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra.
A Brahmin shall perform the Sāṃtapana penance; a Kṣatriya, the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya shall perform half of that; and a Śūdra shall perform one quarter of it.

If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should, through negligence, drink water, curd, or milk contained in a vessel belonging to those of the lowest castes (antyaja), [he must perform penance].
For the twice-born, expiation is through the Brahmakūrca fast;
for a Śūdra, it is through fasting as well as by giving gifts according to his capacity.
O best of the twice-born, if one should somehow eat the food of a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance,
he becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
One should eat a single morsel at a time of either cow-urine or barley-gruel;
one should designate that as the vow for one who remains under restraint for ten days.
But where a Caṇḍāla dwells in a house, [the twice-born] do not perform [rites] because of their lack of knowledge;
however, once he is known, the twice-born show favor to one who has approached them for refuge.
Those who have mastered the Vedas, chanting the dharmas that have issued from the mouth of the Sage,
shall rescue him as he falls from the mixture of sin— those knowers of dharma.
One should consume curd, ghee, milk, cow urine, and barley gruel together with all [of these]; and one should perform immersion [in water] at the three junctions of the day.
For three days he should eat with curd, and for three days he should eat with clarified butter;
for three days he should eat with milk—thus for three days at a time with each one.
One should not eat food that is corrupted by its nature, nor that which is leavings, nor that defiled by insects;
however, one may consume three palas of curd, one pala of milk, and one pala of clarified butter.
Purification for both copper and brass is achieved with ashes;
for clothes, by washing with water; and for earthenware, by discarding it.
Having placed safflower, molasses, cotton, salt, oil,
and clarified butter at the door, one should place the grain and kindle the fire within the house.
Thus purified, he should thereafter perform the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) of the Brahmins;
he should give thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the learned Brahmins.
It is purified by re-plastering, digging, burnt offerings, and recitation;
furthermore, for Brahmins who maintain the sacred fires, no defect of the ground exists.
If one has contact with Caṇḍālas for a month, or even for half a month,
one becomes purified by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel for half a month.
A washerwoman, a leather-worker, a hunter, and a basket-maker— if she stays unrecognized in the house of one belonging to the four castes— Pṣ 6.44.
Having ascertained [the nature of the offense], one should perform the expiation for the previously mentioned [offense] as exactly half;
one should not set fire to the house, but should carry out all the rest.
If a Caṇḍāla should enter the interior of anyone’s house,
he must be expelled from that dwelling, and one should discard the earthenware vessels.
A vessel that has been filled with liquids should never be abandoned;
likewise, one should sprinkle the house with water mixed with cow dung.
When a worm arises from the opening of a wound in a Brāhmaṇa, where pus and blood have accumulated,
what should be the expiation for him?
Having bathed and drunk cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk,
and clarified butter for three days, one who has been defiled by worms becomes pure.
A Kṣatriya, having given five māṣas of gold,
should likewise prescribe a cow as the sacrificial fee for a Vaiśya and a fast;
for Śūdras there shall be no fast, for a Śūdra is purified by giving.
"That which the gods upon earth call 'unbroken' (acchidram) is a sentence."
Having bowed with one's head, it should be accepted, for that indeed yields the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whatever flaw there may be in recitation, whatever flaw in austerity, and whatever flaw in the performance of a sacrificial rite—[that is all remedied by this].
Everything provided by Brahmins becomes free from flaw,
even in times of disease, calamity, exhaustion, famine, or likewise during a violent upheaval.
Fasting, vows, and burnt offerings are indeed accomplished through the agency of the twice-born;
or else, when the Brahmins are satisfied, they bestow grace upon everything.
One obtains all desires in this world through those things prepared by the twice-born.
Likewise, favor is prescribed for the weak, as well as for children and the elderly.
If it were otherwise than this, there would be a fault; therefore, it is not considered a favor.
[This applies] whether out of affection, or greed, or fear, or even through ignorance.
But those who show favor to such people, that sin passes to them;
for those who preach restrictive rules when the dissolution of the body has arrived.
One should never perform [these acts] while in good health, provided they do not obstruct a great task.
Fools who claim there is no fixed rule regarding one in good health act thus.
Those who create obstacles for such a person fall into an impure hell—
he who, having himself undertaken a vow, shows contempt for a Brāhmaṇa.
His fasting would be in vain; he is not joined with merit. That very restraint (niyama) is to be accepted if even a single twice-born man should speak [of it].
One should act according to the word of the twice-born; otherwise, one becomes a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
Brahmins are a moving shrine, for the virtuous are indeed the embodiment of sacred fords.
By the water of their speech alone, even defiled people are purified;
whatever the Brāhmaṇas speak, the gods consider that to be true.
A Brahmin embodies all the gods; his word is never otherwise.
Fasting, religious observances, ritual bathing, pilgrimage to sacred sites, recitation of mantras, and austerity [are all contained within him].
The fruit belongs entirely to him for whom that which was prepared by a Brahmin is completed.
When food and other such items are infested with insects or defiled by flies and hair, [one should act as follows].
If one should touch water between [mouthfuls], one should touch that food with ashes. Furthermore, the Brahmin who, while eating, touches his foot with his hand [is likewise at fault].
One eats one's own leavings from a vessel released by the hand;
one should not eat while standing on sandals, nor while seated upon a couch.
One should avoid eating in the sight of a dog or a caṇḍāla;
likewise, one should observe the rules regarding food that is forbidden and the purification of food.
Just as it was spoken by Parāśara, so do I speak to you:
food cooked in a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* measure that has been defiled by crows or dogs [is unfit for use].
"By what means is this purified?"—thus one should inquire of the Brāhmaṇas.
However, food that has been pecked at by a crow or licked by a dog need not be discarded if it amounts to a *droṇa*.
By Brahmins who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and who uphold the Dharmaśāstras,
thirty-two *prasthas* are traditionally held to be one *droṇa*, and two *prasthas* are one *āḍhaka*.
Therefore, those who know the Śruti and Smṛti understand that food from a droṇa or an āḍhaka [measure] is pure;
even if it has been licked by a crow or a dog, or smelled by a cow or a donkey, it remains fit for use.
A Brahmin should discard even a very small amount of food; purification occurs when the quantity is one *droṇa* or one *āḍhaka*.
Having removed from the food that portion which has been defiled by saliva, [the remainder may be consumed].
Having sprinkled gold with water, one should heat it with fire alone;
[it is purified] when touched by fire and by the water of gold.
By the chanting of the Veda by Brahmins, that food becomes pure at that very moment;
but how can there be purity in the case of oil or even cow's milk?

In that case, one should discard a small amount [of the substance] and purify it by straining the oil. The purification of cow’s milk is prescribed by means of the flame of fire. (This concludes the section on the purification of substances.)
Now, therefore, follows the purification of substances according to the words of Parāśara: the purification of wooden vessels is held to be by planing.
Bell-metal is purified by ashes; copper is purified by acid.
A woman who does not engage in intercourse is purified by her menses.
One is purified by the current of a river if no [remnants] are seen;
likewise when step-wells, wells, or tanks have been somehow defiled.
Having removed a hundred jars [of impurity], one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
A girl of eight years is a *Gaurī*, while one of nine years is a *Rohiṇī*.
A girl becomes ten years old; beyond that, she is menstruating.
But when the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter [is at fault].
Month after month, her menstrual blood is drunk by the ancestors themselves—
the mother, the father, and likewise the eldest brother.
Three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses:
he who would marry such a girl, and the Brahmin who, deluded by passion, [performs the rite].
For that Brahmin who, being a twice-born man, indulges with a *vṛṣalī* for even a single night, is unfit to be spoken to and is excluded from the company at a meal (*apāṅkteya*). (Purāṇa 7.8)
He who subsists on alms and constantly recites [the sacred texts] is purified in three years. When the sun has set, [if he touches] a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, or a woman...
How is purification prescribed for one who touches a woman who has recently given birth?
By beholding the fire, gold, and the path of the moon.
A Brāhmaṇa woman who has been permitted by a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after performing a ritual bath;
likewise, two Brāhmaṇa women who have become menstruating while touching one another [become pure in the same way].
She should remain without food for that long; by three nights alone she is purified.
If two women—one a Brāhmaṇī and the other a Kṣatriyā—both in their menses touch each other, the former shall perform an Ardhakṛcchra penance, and the latter a single quarter-penance.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their menses, touch one another, [they must perform penance].

If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another, she who is of the higher caste shall perform a penance of three-quarters of a quarter, and she who is of the lower caste shall perform a full quarter.
A woman of the first [three] classes is purified with difficulty; a Śūdra woman is purified by giving gifts. A menstruating woman who has bathed becomes pure on the fourth day.
One should perform rites for the gods and ancestors and other such ceremonies once the menstrual flow has ceased;
however, that flow which occurs daily in women due to illness is not subject to this rule.
She does not become impure by that [menstrual flow]; therefore, it is considered fit for evening meals (*vaikālika*). A woman of virtuous conduct remains so as long as the flow of blood continues.
A woman who has ceased her menses is fit for approach; indeed, she is also fit for household duties.
On the first day [of her period] she is a Caṇḍālī, and on the second day she is a slayer of a Brahmin.
On the third day she is called a washerwoman; on the fourth day she becomes pure.
When a bath is required due to illness, one who is not ill must bathe ten times.

Having bathed again and again, that afflicted twice-born man should touch him; then he shall become pure, even if he has been touched by one who is impure from food remnants, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra.
Having fasted for one night, one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Upon being touched by a Śūdra who is not rendered impure by food remnants, bathing is prescribed.
One who has been touched by that leavings [of food] should perform a Prājāpatya penance.
Bell-metal is purified with ashes, provided it is not stained by liquor.
An object touched by even a mere trace of *surā* liquor is purified by heating over fire and scrubbing with a stone;
the same applies to bell-metal vessels that have been smelled by a cow or defiled by dogs and crows.
Those items that have been defiled by the remnants of a Śūdra are purified by ten alkaline substances;
likewise, one who has rinsed their mouth or washed their feet in a vessel made of white copper (kāṃsya) must purify it in the same manner.
Having buried iron for six months in the earth and then having extracted it, one should bring it back;
for iron objects and for tin, purification is performed in fire.
One should wash with water these items: ivory, bone, as well as beeswax, silver, golden vessels, and bowls made of gems or stone.
Furthermore, for stone, purification is declared to be by scrubbing;
for earthenware, purification is by burning, and for grains, it is also by winnowing.
The purification of bamboo, bark, rags, linen, cotton cloth, wool, nets,
and cloths is held to be achieved by sprinkling.
For items made of muñja grass, household utensils, winnowing baskets, hemp, fruits,
hides, grass, wood, and ropes, sprinkling with water is considered the required purification.
Cushions such as those stuffed with tūlī-wool, as well as dyed garments and the like,
attain purity by being dried in the sun and then sprinkled with water.
Manu has declared that cats, flies, insects, moths, worms,
and frogs do not cause one to become impure from food remnants (ucchiṣṭa), even though they touch what is pure and what is impure.
Manu has declared that water which has returned to the earth after touching it, as well as mutual droplets [from the mouth],
the remnants of food, and oily substances, do not constitute *ucchiṣṭa* (remnants of a meal).

According to the Dharma, they know that there is no "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa) status in the case of betel, sugarcane, and fruit; likewise when one has smeared oneself with oil after eating, or when partaking of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), or at a Soma sacrifice.
Roads, mud, water, boats, paths, and grass are purified by the wind and the sun; likewise, structures built with baked bricks are purified by the same means.
A continuous stream that is not defiled, dust raised by the wind,
and women who are aged or young— these are never considered impure.
In the event of the ruin of one's country, during exile, or even amidst diseases and calamities, one should certainly protect one's own body and so forth; thereafter, one should practice dharma.
By whatever means possible— whether gentle or harsh—
one who is capable should rescue oneself from distress and practice righteousness. Once the time of calamity has passed, one should then attend to the rules of purity and proper conduct.
One should subsequently effect purification and, once restored to health, practice dharma.
(Pṣ 7.38cd) If death should occur unintentionally while [cattle] are being tied with a tethering rope, how is there expiation for a sin committed unintentionally? (Pṣ 8.1ab–cd)
One should confess one's own sin to those who are learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, who understand the Dharmaśāstras, and who are Brahmins devoted to their own duties.

Those Brahmins who, through ignorance, perform the Sāvitrī, the Gāyatrī, the twilight devotions, and the fire-ritual merely as a matter of name are practitioners of agriculture; they are Brahmins in name only.
For those who lack vows, who lack sacred mantras, and who subsist merely by their birth—
though they may assemble by the thousands— an assembly (*pariṣad*) does not exist.
Whatever those who are deluded by darkness, fools, and ignorant of the Dharma, proclaim—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon the speaker thereof.
He who prescribes an expiation without having understood the treatises on Dharma shall himself become purified through that very expiation, while the sin goes to the assembly.
That which four or even three who have reached the further shore of the Vedas may declare is to be known as Dharma; it is not so by thousands of others.
Evil trembles before those who speak of the true qualities of reality, who proclaim the Dharma while seeking the path of valid cognition.
Just as water situated upon a stone is purified by wind and sun,
so too shall one’s evil deed be destroyed through the instruction of the assembly.
It does not go to the doer, nor does it go to the assembly;
through contact with the wind, the sun, and so forth, sin perishes like water.
Whether there be four or even three Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and maintain the sacred fires— whoever are capable [of judging], they are designated as an assembly (pariṣad).
Those who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet are otherwise masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—
whether five or three such persons who know the Dharma— that is proclaimed to be an assembly (pariṣad).
Even a single person may constitute an assembly for sages who know the self, for twice-born men who perform sacrifices, and for those who have been consecrated in the Vedic vows.
The five types previously mentioned by me, or in their absence, three; those who are content with their own livelihood—such an assembly is proclaimed as a *pariṣad*.
But from this point forward, those brahmins who merely bear the name have no status as an assembly, even if they are multiplied by a thousand.
Just as an elephant made of wood, or a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
As a village site that is empty, as a well that is without water,
and as an oblation offered where there is no fire, so is a Brahmin who lacks the sacred mantras.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, and as a barren cow is fruitless,
and just as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by many constituent parts,
so too is Brahminhood produced by means of purificatory rites preceded by mantras.
Those twice-born who merely bear the name of a brahmin yet prescribe penance [for others],
being themselves performers of evil deeds, have all gone together to hell.
Those twice-born who recite the Veda and those who are devoted to the five sacrifices—
they rescue the three worlds, even if they are attached to the five senses.
A fire that has been properly kindled in cremation grounds is a blazing consumer of all things;
likewise, a Brahmin learned in the Vedas is a deity, even if he consumes all things.
Just as all impure things are cast into water,
even so, O twice-born one, should one cast all sin into the fire.
A Brahmin devoid of the Gāyatrī becomes more impure even than a Śūdra;
those twice-born ones who know the reality of the Brahman through the Gāyatrī are honored by people.
Even a twice-born man of bad character is worthy of honor, but not a Śūdra who has conquered his senses.
Who would abandon a vicious cow to milk a she-ass, however well-behaved?
The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas,
are said to possess the supreme Dharma in whatever they declare, even if spoken in jest.
One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (aṅga), a reciter of the Dharma,
and three from among the principal stages of life— this assembly is "at least ten."
Having remained with the king’s permission, one should prescribe the expiation (*prāyaścitta*);
one must not perform it oneself, but rather a small fee (*niṣkṛti*) should be paid.
Whatever a king desires to do by transgressing against those Brahmins,
that sin becomes tenfold and follows after the king.
One should always offer an expiation (prāyaścitta) before a temple of the deity;
then, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for oneself, one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas (Sāvitrī).
Having shaved his head together with the top-knot, he should immerse himself in water at the three junctions of the day;
he should dwell among cows at night and follow after them during the day.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking.
One should drink water when [the cows] are drinking; one should lie down when they are lying down.
One should rescue with all one's strength a cow that has fallen or is stuck in the mud.
He who would sacrifice his life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
he is the protector of both the cow and the Brahmin.
One should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance in proportion to the value of the stolen cattle;
thereafter, one should divide that Prājāpatya Kṛcchra into four types.
For one day he shall eat only a single meal; for one day he shall eat only at night;
for one day he shall eat only what is unasked for; and for one day he shall subsist on air alone.
For two days he should eat only one meal a day, and for two days he should take a single meal;
for two days he should be one who does not beg, and for two days he should subsist on air alone.
For three days one should eat only a single meal, for three days one should eat only at night;
for three days one should not beg for food, and for three days one should subsist on air alone.
For four days one should eat only a single meal, for four days one should eat only at night;
for four days one should be a non-seeker of alms, and for four days one should subsist on air alone.
When the penance has been performed, one should then feed Brahmins;
the twice-born man should give sacrificial fees to the Brahmins and recite purificatory prayers.
Having fed Brāhmaṇas, the cow-killer is purified; of this there is no doubt.
For the purpose of protecting cows, one does not incur sin through confining or tethering them.
One should not consider that as their killing, whether done intentionally or unintentionally.
If one should cause [an animal] to fall by striking it with something other than a staff after [the initial strike],
then the expiation prescribed for killing a cow must be performed twice.
Imprisonment, confinement, the yoke, and execution—these are the four kinds [of punishment].
One should undergo one quarter [of the penalty] for imprisonment, and two quarters for confinement.
If a horse should stumble and fall, one must perform the entire expiation;
likewise if it falls in a cow-pen, in a house, in a difficult place, or on uneven ground.

In rivers and oceans, but not at the mouths of other rivers; in a burnt region, cows that have died are called "stambhana" (obstructive). Pṣ9.5. Pṣ9.5cd/.dagdha.deśe.mṛtā.gāvaḥ.stambhanād.rodha.ucyate.// (Cows that die in a burnt area are called rodha because of their obstruction.)
If a cow should die while bound in a house or even in a forest by means of a yoke-tie, a tethering rope, a cord, or by neck-ornaments and decorations; Pṣ9.6cd: [then the following penance applies].
One should know that very same thing to be bondage, whether it is caused by desire or by lack of desire;
such as being oppressed by men with a plow, a cart, in a crowd, or on one's back.
The master of the cows meets with death; such is the nature of the yoke-tie.
Whether intoxicated, negligent, insane, conscious, or even unconscious.
Whether acting out of desire or without desire, one who commits an act of anger should be struck with staffs or stones;
whether he is wounded or even killed, for that [act] is the cause of his downfall.

If he has fainted or fallen, or has been struck by a staff, yet rises and proceeds [to his destination] after five, seven, or ten [leagues], or if he should take a morsel of food or even drink water;
