If he was previously afflicted by disease, no expiation is required.
For killing an embryo while it is still in the form of a *piṇḍa*, one quarter of the penance is prescribed; for an embryo that has attained the stage of *garbha*, two quarters are prescribed;
and for killing an insentient embryo, the vow is declared to be three-quarters less.
For a one-quarter offense, there shall be the shaving of the hair on the limbs; for a two-quarter offense, the beard as well;
for a three-quarter offense, everything except the top-knot; but for a complete offense, the top-knot must also be shaved.
For one-quarter of the penance, a pair of garments; for two-quarters, a bronze vessel;
for three-quarters, one should give a bull; and for the fourth part, two cows are prescribed.
But if he is seen with all his limbs fully formed and endowed with consciousness,
complete in every major and minor limb, he shall perform the cow-vow (go-vrata) for double the duration.
If one strikes cows with a stone or a staff,
he shall perform one quarter-penance (pāda) for breaking a horn, and two quarters for injuring an eye.
If a cow has been struck by a stone or a staff,
one should perform one quarter-penance for breaking its horn, and two quarters for injuring its eye.
For striking the tail, one-quarter of the *pāda-kṛcchra* penance is prescribed; for breaking a bone, two quarters;
for cutting off an ear, three quarters; and for causing death, one should perform the full penance.
In the case of the breaking of a horn, the breaking of a bone, and likewise the breaking of the hip—
if the animal lives for six months, no penance is prescribed.
When a wound has been treated, an oil massage should be performed by hand;
furthermore, fodder should be provided until the animal has regained its full strength.
As long as all its limbs are complete, so long should the man nourish it;
having first paid homage to the form of the cow as the Brahmin, he should then dismiss it.
If he should have his limbs incomplete or his body deficient due to an imperfect creation,
then one should prescribe an expiation for him on account of that killing of a cow.
One who, out of forceful intent, causes a cow to be killed by means of wood, clods of earth, stones, or even a weapon— for him, one should prescribe purification.
One should perform the Sāṃtapana penance for killing a wooden post, the Prājāpatya for a clod of earth,
the Tapta-kṛcchra for a stone, and the Atikṛcchra for a weapon.
In the Pañcasaṃtapanakṛcchra there are five cows; likewise, in the Prājāpatya, there are three.
In the Tapta-kṛcchra there are eight, and in the Atikṛcchra, there are thirteen.
For the killing of living beings, one should give a substitute for that [life];
or one should pay its equivalent value—thus Manu has declared.
Except for branding and marking, as well as for the purpose of transport and release,
and for the sake of protection at night, there is no offense in confining or binding [cattle].
In cases of excessive burning, excessive carrying of loads, as well as piercing the nose,
and traveling over rivers or mountains, one should prescribe an expiation.

In the case of excessive burning, one should perform one quarter of the penance; in the case of a carriage, two quarters; for a blow with the nose, one should perform three-quarters; but for a full strike, one should perform the whole.
"But from being burnt while restrained by the yoke, the ox perishes;
for Parāśara has declared this regarding a single hoof according to the rule."
Confinement, binding, carrying loads, striking,
driving through difficult terrain, and the use of a yoke— these six are the causes of death.
If a cow or beast dies while its limbs are tightly bound by a tether or rope, the owner of the dwelling shall be sinful; he deserves half of the penance.
One should not [bind] with coconut fibers, nor with hemp-hair, nor even with muñja-grass, nor with bark-fiber chains.
Cows should not be tied up with these [materials]; even if they have been tied, one should remain holding an axe.

One should bind the cow, the sacrificial animal, with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass, facing it toward the south. There is no need for expiation when the animal is burnt by fire caught in its tethering rope.
If wood should be present there, how would the expiation be performed?
By reciting the purifying goddess, one is liberated from that sin.
By urging [cattle] into wells or ponds, by causing them to fall during the felling of trees,
or by selling them for the consumption of cattle, one thereby incurs the guilt of killing a cow.
But when anyone who has been propitiated becomes one whose ranks are broken—
whether his ears and heart are shattered, or he is submerged in the narrowness of a well— then [the consequences follow].
If one dies there after climbing out of a well, or if his neck or feet are broken,
he shall perform three-quarters of the penance.
This applies also in the case of digging a well, constructing a bank, building a bridge over a river, or at water-stations (prapās).
For those who have perished in waters, no expiation is prescribed.
In the case of digging a well, a pond, or a long trench,
as well as in other dharma-digging projects, no expiation is prescribed.
For a man who desires to dig a pit at the door of a house or within his own dwellings— for such excavations made for one's own purposes or for the house— one should prescribe an expiation.
For those who die at night, or are confined by fetters, or killed by serpents or tigers,
or perish by fire or lightning, no expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed.
In the case of those killed by a flood of arrows during the destruction of a village, by the collapse of a house,
or by excessive rain, no expiation is prescribed.
For those killed in battle, those who have perished in their homes by fire,
and those who died in forest fires or village massacres— for these, no expiation is prescribed.
When a cow is restrained for the purpose of medical treatment or to deliver a dead fetus,
if she should perish despite the effort being made, no expiation is prescribed.
One should prescribe an expiation for the binding or even the confinement of many people who have been injured,
as well as for a physician’s improper treatment.
And when cattle or bulls meet with misfortune, all those people who were looking on and did not prevent it shall incur the sin of that slaughter.

When a single person has been killed by many acting together, and it is not known from the impact of the blow who specifically struck him, O King, the slayer must be identified through divine means by those appointed by you and then brought to justice.
If some single woman is killed by many through fate,
they shall each perform one quarter of the penance for the killing individually.
If blood is seen, [the victim] has been killed; if seized by disease, he becomes emaciated.
Saliva appears when one is bitten; such is the method of investigation.
Or even if urged for the sake of food, he does not travel on the road;
thus it was said by Manu alone, who knew all the scriptures.
The expiation prescribed by him is as follows: a cow-killer shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
for the sake of preserving his hair, he shall perform double the vow.
When a vow is prescribed that is to be performed twice, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be doubled;
this applies whether it be a king, a prince, or a Brahmin who is deeply learned in the scriptures.
Without performing the shaving of his hair, one should prescribe an expiation for him:
having pulled out all the hair, he should have two finger-breadths cut off.
In this same way, the shaving of the head is prescribed for women and young girls;
however, there is no shaving of the hair for a woman, nor should she sleep or eat at a distance [from the funeral pyre].
One should not stay overnight in a cow-pen, nor should one follow cows during the day;
likewise, one should avoid [staying] at river confluences and especially in forests.
Women do not wear deerskin as clothing; they should observe only the vow [of celibacy].
It is said that they should bathe at the three junctions of the day and likewise perform the worship of the gods.
In the midst of their kinsmen, their penance shall consist of the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such observances;
they should remain constantly in their homes, pure and practicing self-restraint.
He who, having committed the slaughter of a cow in this world, desires to conceal it,
goes without doubt to the terrible hell known as Kālasūtra.
Released from that hell, that man is born in the world of mortals as a eunuch,
miserable, and afflicted with leprosy for seven births.
Therefore, one should reveal one's sin and constantly practice one's own duty;
one should avoid excessive anger toward women, children, servants, cattle, and Brahmins.
I shall now declare the beneficial expiation for all the four castes.
And for approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for purification.

One should decrease the morsels by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase them during the bright fortnight; on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa fast.
One should indeed determine the size of a morsel to be equal to a hen’s egg;
otherwise, due to the fault of improper disposition, there is neither dharma nor purification.
Then, once the penance has been performed, one should provide a meal for Brahmins;
furthermore, one should give two cows and a pair of garments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
If a twice-born man approaches a Caṇḍālī or a Śvapākī,
he shall fast for three nights according to the instruction of the Brahmins.
Having shaved his hair along with the top-knot (śikhā), he should perform two Prājāpatya penances;
he should give two cows as a sacrificial fee—thus Pārāśara has declared purification.
If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya has sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman,
he should perform two Prājāpatya penances and give away two pairs of cattle.
If a Śūdra has sexual intercourse with a Śvapākī or a Caṇḍālī,
he shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give a pair of four cows as a gift.
If one should approach his mother, or likewise his sister or his own daughter,
having approached these through delusion, he shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
One should perform three cāndrāyaṇa penances; one is purified by the excision of the penis.
And likewise, for sexual intercourse with one's mother's sister, there shall be the excision of his own penis.
But he who should approach [her] out of ignorance shall perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
he should give a pair of ten cows, for this is purification, as Pārāśara has declared.
Having approached the wife of his father, or one born of his mother’s kinsman, or the wife of his teacher, or his daughter-in-law, or likewise the wife of his brother; Pṣ 10.12.
If one has sexual intercourse with a maternal aunt or a woman of the same lineage (sagotrā), one should perform three Prājāpatya penances;
he should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and he is thereby purified—of this there is no doubt.
Having approached female animals for sexual intercourse— such as a buffalo, a camel, a female monkey, as well as a female donkey or a sow— one should perform the Prājāpatya vow.

One who has approached a cow is purified by a three-night fast upon giving a single cow to a Brāhmaṇa; however, one who has approached a female buffalo, a female camel, or a female donkey is purified in a single day and night.
In times of plague or battle, during famine or the destruction of people,
or when captured as a prisoner and afflicted by fear, one should always look upon one’s own wife.
If a woman enters into association with Caṇḍālas,
she should then assemble ten eminent Brahmins and disclose her own transgression.
In a well that reaches up to the neck, filled with a mire of cow-dung and water,
one should remain there without food and emerge after a day and night.
Having shaved the head including the top-knot, one should eat a meal of barley gruel.
Having fasted for three nights, he should dwell in water for one night.
Having boiled the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper,
along with gold and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should drink the water.
Thereafter, she should subsist on a single meal until she becomes menstruating;
for as long as she performs that vow, she shall dwell outside [the community].
Then, when the penance has been performed, one should feed Brāhmaṇas;
Pārāśara has declared that purity is attained by giving a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee.
For women of the four castes, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa vows [are prescribed as penance].
As is the earth, so is a woman; therefore, one should not defile her.
If a woman has been enjoyed by force—having been captured as a prisoner, killed, or bound out of fear—she is purified by performing the *Sāṃtapana* penance; so said Pārāśara.
But a woman who has been enjoyed only once against her will by those of evil deeds shall be purified by the Prājāpatya penance and by the flow of menses.
Half of the body of that man falls [with him] whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no atonement is prescribed.
One who mutters the Gāyatrī should perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance;
[the ingredients for which are] the Gāyatrī, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass.
Fasting for one night is recorded as the *sāṃtapana* penance.
If she conceives a child by a paramour when her husband is dead, missing, or unaccounted for, [this is the rule].
One should abandon her in another kingdom—her, who is fallen and a doer of evil;
for when a Brāhmaṇa woman goes forth united with another man.
She who, out of lust or delusion, departs having abandoned her kinsmen, children, and husband, is declared lost; there shall be no returning for her again.
But that woman who, overcome by intoxication and delusion, strikes others with a staff or other implements out of anger, is lost in the next world, and especially among human beings.
If she has gone [to her husband] for a second time, there shall be a return;
however, when the tenth day has arrived, no expiation is prescribed.
One should not abandon a woman for ten days; likewise, one should abandon her if she has lost her sense of sacred learning (*śruti*).
The husband shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance, and his kinsmen shall perform half a *kṛcchra*.
Having eaten from or drunk from their vessels, one is purified after a day and night. But when a Brāhmaṇī woman, being unguarded, goes with another man...
Having gone [to another], she goes to a hundred men; however, her kinsmen (gotriṇaḥ) should abandon her.
If a man should go to her house, that house would become impure.
That which is the house of the husband’s mother is indeed the house of the paramour;
having scraped that house, one should afterwards sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

One should discard a vessel made of clay, and one should purify clothing and wood. All ritual materials, including those derived from fruits, should be cleansed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and cow hair.

Copper vessels [are purified] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and bronze vessels with ashes ten times over; the Brahmin should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as prescribed by the Brahmins.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and perform two Prājāpatya penances.
For others, purification consists of fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow.
Through fasts, meritorious vows, ritual bathing, the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), worship, and so forth;
and through recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), compassion, and gifts, the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are purified.
Space, wind, fire, and water on the ground are pure;
likewise, *darbha* grasses do not become defiled in sacrifices, just like the sacrificial cups (*camasa*).
Impure semen, beef, or even the food of a *caṇḍāla*— [these do not defile].
If a Brahmin has eaten [forbidden food], he shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
In the same way, a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya should perform half of a Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
a Śūdra, when he eats in this manner, should perform a Prājāpatya penance.
A Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); a twice-born man should drink the Brahmakūrca.
Or, they should give one, two, three, or four cows, respectively, according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇa.

The food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), and the food of one whose food is unfit to be eaten; food that is suspected [of being impure], prohibited food, and likewise the leavings of another; 11.4ab–cd.
If a Brahmin has eaten [forbidden food] either through ignorance or due to distress, he should,
upon realizing it, perform the purifying Kṛcchra known as the Brahmakūrca.
When food has been defiled by the remnants of a meal left by children, mongooses, or cats, it becomes pure after being sprinkled with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water; of this there is no doubt.
When Brahmins are seated in a single row for a communal meal,
if even one person should set aside his vessel, the remaining food must not be eaten.
If a Brahmin should eat the leavings in that row out of delusion,
he should perform the *kṛcchra* penance as well as the *sāṃtapana*.
Pīyūṣa (unripened milk), white garlic, the vṛntāka fruit, gṛñjana, palāṇḍu,
the resin of trees, and mushrooms belonging to the gods (or growing on sacred ground).
If a twice-born man consumes camel’s milk or ewe’s milk through ignorance,
he is purified by fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having eaten a frog as well as the flesh of a mouse, a Brahmin,
upon realizing it, is purified by subsisting on barley-gruel for a day and a night.
A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are diligent in their duties and pure in their vows—
food from their houses may always be eaten by the twice-born at rites for the gods and the ancestors.
Clarified butter, oil, as well as milk, and food cooked with fat—
having gone to the bank of a river, a Brahmin may eat such food even if it was prepared by a Śūdra.
A Brahmin should avoid from afar that Śūdra who is constantly devoted to liquor and meat and who engages in base occupations, as he would a dog-cooker.
A twice-born man should never abandon those Śūdras who are devoted to serving the twice-born, who abstain from liquor and meat, and who are constantly intent upon their own duties.
If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka),
how should one prescribe the expiation (prāyaścitta) for them according to each respective caste?
Purification from the birth-impurity of a Śūdra occurs through eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī;
for a Vaiśya, it is by five thousand, and for a Kṣatriya, by three thousand.
When one eats at the house of a Brāhmaṇa, one should cause two thousand [cows] to be given;
or else, one is purified by the Vāmadevya Sāman alone.
Manu has declared that dried food, cow's milk, and oil obtained from the house of a Śūdra are fit to be eaten,
provided they have been cooked in the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
If a Brahmin has eaten in the house of a Śūdra during times of distress,
he shall be purified by mental anguish or by reciting the Drupadā verses one hundred times.
A slave, a barber, a cowherd, a family friend, and a sharecropper— among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
A son born from a Śūdra maiden who has been consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Dāsa through that consecration; however, if he is not consecrated, he is a Nāpita.
The son who is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra maiden is to be known as a Gopāla; he may be fed by Brahmins, without a doubt.
One born from a Vaiśya maiden who has been consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa is to be known as an Ārdhika; he is to be fed by the Brāhmaṇas, without a doubt.
Pṣ 11.25ab: Water, curd, ghee, or milk that has been placed in a vessel used for forbidden foods— Pṣ 11.25cd: If one consumes these unintentionally, what should the expiation be?
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who approaches [for sexual intercourse with an unprotected woman],
the expiation for one of the twice-born castes is the Brahmakūrca fast.
For Śūdras, there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts.
Even a dog-cooker (outcaste) may be purified by the Brahmakūrca rite performed for a day and night.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
this is designated as the "five products of the cow" (*pañcagavya*), which is purifying and cleanses one of sin.
Cow’s urine from a black cow, cow dung from a white one,
milk from a copper-colored cow, and curd from a red cow are taken.
Ghee should be taken from a tawny cow, or all [the products] may be from a tawny cow alone. One should provide one *pala* of urine and half the size of a thumb of cow dung.
One should give seven palas of milk; it is said that three palas of curd are to be given;
one pala of ghee should be given; and one pala of kuśa-water.
Having taken cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārām," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhi krāvṇaḥ."
With the mantra "Thou art brilliance, thou art pure," he should place the clarified butter; with "Thee for the God," the kuśa-water;
and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), purified by the Ṛgvedic verse, he should set down in the vicinity of the fire.

Having stirred [the water] with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭha," one should consecrate it with the mantra "mānastoke. Furthermore, there should be seven blades of *darbha* grass that are uncut at the tips and as bright as a parrot's plumage.
Having extracted [the dregs] with these [mantras], one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the rule,
using the mantras "irāvatī," "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and "mā nas toke," which are auspicious.
With these [mantras] alone should one offer the oblation, and the twice-born should drink the remnant of what has been offered;
having stirred it with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), and likewise having churned it with the *praṇava*.
Having extracted [the water] with the *praṇava* alone, one should drink it with the *praṇava* as well;
for whatever sin resides within the body of embodied beings, even that which has entered the bones, [is removed].
The Brahmakūrca burns away everything, just as a blazing fire consumes fuel;
it is a purifier in the three worlds, presided over by the deities.
Varuṇa resides in cow urine, and the bearer of oblations (Agni) in cow dung;
Vāyu is declared to be in curd, Soma in milk, and the Sun in clarified butter.
One should know that water which has fallen from the mouth into a vessel while drinking is unfit to be drunk; having drunk it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a twice-born man sees a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well,
or if he drinks water that has become impure by contact with fallen bones, skin, and the like, [he must perform purification].
A human corpse, a crow, a village pig, a donkey, a camel,
a gavaya, a supratīka, a peacock, and likewise a rhinoceros— these [are forbidden].
If one sinks into a well containing the skin of a tiger, a bear, or a lion, or if one has drunk the water of a contaminated pond; Pṣ 11.43cd. [one must perform purification].
By this entire sequence, the expiation for a man shall be determined in its proper order:
a Brahmin is purified in three nights, while a Kṣatriya is purified in two days.
A Vaiśya, however, is purified in one day; a Śūdra becomes pure by night.
Of one who has desisted from cooking for others and of one who delights in cooking for others.
Having eaten the food of an *apaca*, a twice-born man shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance;
and as for the gift given by an *apaca*, how can there be any fruit for the giver?
Both the giver and the receiver—these two go to hell;
having taken the sacred fire and established it, he who does not perform the five sacrifices.
He who has desisted from cooking for others is proclaimed by the sages as one who,
having himself performed the five sacrifices, subsists on the food of others.
That brahmin who, though devoted to the householder’s duty, constantly rises early in the morning and is intent on cooking for others, yet gives nothing away, is devoid of merit.

The sages who knew the true essence of dharma have proclaimed that there is no dharma other than that which exists in each respective age and among those specific twice-born ones belonging to those ages.
One must not utter censure against them, for those twice-born ones are the very form of the Yugas.
Having uttered the sound "hum" to a Brāhmaṇa, or the word "thou" to one who is superior, [one incurs great sin].
Having bathed and remained standing for the remainder of the day, he should appease [the teacher] by offering salutations;
even if he has struck him with a blade of grass or bound him around the neck with a garment.

Even after winning by means of a dispute, one should appease the opponent by bowing down. However, for threatening [another], the penance is one day and night; for causing him to fall to the ground, it is three nights.

In the case of blood [on the teeth], one should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance; if the blood is internal, the *kṛcchra*. One who subsists on a handful of food for nine days shall be performing the *atikṛcchra*.
One who fasts for three nights performs what is called the *atikṛcchra* penance;
this is prescribed when a mixture of all kinds of sins has occurred.
The Gāyatrī, when repeated ten thousand times, is the supreme means of purification.

(Pṣ 11.56ab) If one sees a bad dream, or after vomiting, or after the rite of shaving, or after sexual intercourse, or after exposure to the smoke from a funeral pyre, bathing alone is prescribed. (Pṣ 12.1)
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or even that which has been touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again.
The deer-skin, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the religious observances—
all these are set aside for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.
One who consumes feces or urine shall perform a *prājāpatya* penance for purification;
furthermore, by consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) after bathing, one shall become pure.
Regarding those who have fallen from their caste due to drowning, fire, suicide by jumping from a precipice, renunciation of the world, or fasting unto death—
how is their purification prescribed?
By performing two *prājāpatya* penances, by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
and by the gift of eleven bulls, those three castes are purified.
I shall declare the penance for a Brāhmaṇa: having gone to a forest crossroads and shaved his head including the top-knot, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee; so Svāyambhuva has declared purification. By that, one is released from that sin and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
The wise have proclaimed five meritorious baths:
the Agneya, the Varuna, the Brahma, the Vayavya, and the Divya.

The bath with ashes is that of Agni; the bath after plunging into water is that of Varuṇa; the bath with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭha" is that of Brahmā; and the bath with the dust raised by cows is remembered as that of Vāyu.
But that which is performed with rain accompanied by heat is called divine bathing;
having bathed there, a person becomes as one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā.
All the gods, together with the hosts of ancestors, follow a twice-born man as he goes to bathe;
transformed into the nature of wind, they go along, afflicted by thirst and seeking water.
When the wringing out of the garment is performed, they turn back disappointed;
therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having performed the libation for the ancestors.
He who, having placed [the offering] in the pores of his skin, satisfies the ancestors with sesame seeds—
by him the ancestors are satisfied with blood and with filth.
He who shakes his hair after bathing, or who discharges filth [from his body],
or even one who sips water while standing in the water— such a twice-born man is excluded from the rites of the ancestors and the gods.
Having covered one's head or neck, or with the lower garment tucked up or the topknot loosened,
or even without the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one remains impure even after performing the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

One standing on land should not perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) while remaining in the water, nor one standing in the water while remaining on land. Having touched both [the water and the ground], one who has performed the sipping becomes pure in both places.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road,
and after putting on another garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
Upon sneezing, spitting, having food remaining between the teeth, speaking untruth,
or conversing with those who have fallen from their caste, one should touch the right ear.
“Prabhāsa and other sacred fords, as well as the Gaṅgā and other rivers,
reside within the right ear of a Brāhmaṇa,” so Manu declared.
Fire, water, the Vedas, Soma, Sūrya, and likewise Vāyu [reside there].
But all [the fires] of a Brahmin indeed abide in the right ear.
Bathing during the day, purified by the rays of the sun, is praised;
bathing at night is not recommended, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [during an eclipse].
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and burnt offerings should be performed during the appearance of Rāhu;
however, at other times the night is impure, therefore one should avoid it.
The Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are the deities; they all dissolve into Soma. Therefore, a gift should indeed be given at that libation.

At a *khala-yajña*, at a wedding, at the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*), and likewise during an eclipse, the giving of gifts is indeed prescribed for the night; it is not ordained for any other occasion.
Giving is praised at the birth of a son, during a sacrifice, as well as in rites for the deceased, and upon the sight of Rāhu; it is not [praised] otherwise at night.
The two middle watches of the night should be known as the "great night" (mahāniśā). During the first and last watches, one should perform bathing as prescribed for the day.
A sacred tree, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, an outcaste, and a seller of Soma [are places where bathing is forbidden].
But having touched these, a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the water with his clothes on.
Before the collection of the bones, one should perform a bath after weeping;
however, for a Brahmin within ten days [of death], there shall be only sipping of water (ācamana).
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, all water is equal to the Gaṅgā;
the same is declared regarding the eclipse of the moon for rites such as bathing and giving gifts.
When a twice-born man performs a bath purified by *kuśa* grass, or touches water with *kuśa*,
or draws up water with *kuśa*, that water becomes equal to the drinking of Soma.
Those who have fallen away from the fire-rituals, those who have abandoned the worship of the twilights (saṃdhyā),
and those who do not study the Veda— all these are declared to be vṛṣalas.
Therefore, a Brahmin who is especially afraid of a low-born man (vṛṣala) should study at least a portion [of the Veda],
even if he is unable to master it all.
Even for one who constantly studies, mutters prayers, or offers oblations, if he is nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra,
no upward path exists for him.
Eating the food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together with a Śūdra,
and receiving knowledge from a Śūdra— even these cause one to fall, even if one is blazing with spiritual merit.
That twice-born man who constantly causes food to be cooked by a Śūdra woman, and whose housewife is a Śūdra woman,
is excluded from the ancestors and the gods, and he goes to the Raurava hell.
A twice-born man whose body is nourished by the food of a Śūdra— having grown fat on the food of those who eat the remnants of the dead or the impurity of birth—
I do not know what various wombs he will enter.
For twelve births he shall be a vulture, for ten births a pig, and for seven births he shall be born in the womb of a dog; thus Manu has declared.
But that Brahmin who, seeking wealth, should offer the oblation for a Śūdra—
the Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra, and the Śūdra becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
Having undertaken the vow of silence, the twice-born man should not speak while seated. For if he should speak while eating, one must avoid that food.
If a Brahmin drinks water from that vessel while only half of the meal has been consumed,
he destroys the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and brings harm upon himself.
But among the Brahmins who are eating, he who first sets down his vessel is a fool and a most sinful man; indeed, he is called a slayer of the Veda (brahmaghna).
When the vessels are still standing, those twice-born who pronounce blessings do not cause the gods to attain satisfaction, and likewise the ancestors depart disappointed.
One should not eat without having bathed, nor without having recited prayers, nor without having offered oblations to the fire;
likewise, one should not eat from the back of a leaf, nor at night without a lamp.

But the householder, endowed with compassion, should contemplate only dharma; being of sound intellect and abiding by justice, he should do so for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those whom he must support.
One must indeed protect oneself by means of wealth acquired through righteous means;
however, he who lives by unrighteous means is excluded from all ritual acts.

The fire-piler, a tawny cow, one who has completed a long sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify merely by being seen; therefore, one should look upon them constantly.
One should keep these things in the house: the fire-drill, a black cat, sandalwood, a fine gem, ghee, sesame seeds, a black antelope skin, and a goat.
Where a hundred cows with a single bull remain unconfined,
that field is proclaimed to be a "go-carma" (cow-hide area), reckoned as ten times [the standard measure].
A mortal is freed from all sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, which arise from the actions of mind, speech, and body, by the gift of this ox-hide.
That gift which is given specifically to a poor householder who is well-versed in the Vedas (śrotriya) brings about auspicious results.
One who seizes land is not purified by means of constructing step-wells, wells, tanks, and the like, nor by hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, nor even by the gift of ten million cows.
Within eighteen days, a menstruating woman should simply bathe;
beyond that, she must observe a three-night period of impurity—so said the sage Uśanas.
A yoke, two yokes, three yokes, and four yokes [should be placed] below,
respectively, for those who are Cāṇḍālas, those who have recently given birth, menstruating women, and the fallen (patita).
Then, by the mere presence [of the corpse], one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. Having bathed, if one has touched [the corpse] through ignorance, one should look at the sun.
A Brāhmaṇa who is weak in knowledge, while water is available in his own hands, drinks it from his mouth; he will certainly be born in the womb of a dog.
But if a man, being angry, should declare that his wife is not to be approached,
yet later desires her again, he should have it proclaimed in the midst of the Brahmins.
One who is exhausted, angry, blinded by darkness, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fear—
if such a person does not perform a meritorious gift, he must undergo a three-day penance.
One should perform ablutions three times a day at the confluence of great rivers;
and at the conclusion of the penance, one should give a cow as a gift and feed ten Brahmins.
Having eaten the food of a Brahmin who is of evil conduct and who practices forbidden acts, a twice-born man should observe a fast for one day.
By eating the food of a Brahmin who follows right conduct and likewise knows the end of the Vedas,
a man is freed from sin within the interval of a day and night.
One who has food remaining above the lips, or food remaining below the lips, or who eats during the menstrual period,
as well as one who dies while in a state of ritual impurity, should perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
One should perform a *kṛcchra* penance, ten thousand recitations of the *Devīsūkta*, two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*),
and twelve ritual baths at a sacred ford (*puṇyatīrtha*) while the head remains unwetted.
For a householder who intentionally causes the emission of semen upon the ground, a single Kṛcchra penance is prescribed as a pilgrimage to a sacred ford (tīrtha-yātrā) extending over two yojanas.
One who possesses the fourfold knowledge should recite the mantra of the Goddess one thousand times along with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the rule for the slayer of a Brahmin.
One should prescribe the journey to the bridge over the ocean as the penance;
on the path of that bridge-construction, one should beg for alms from the four castes.
Having avoided those engaged in forbidden occupations, and being without an umbrella or sandals, [he should say]:
"I am indeed a doer of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins."
"I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms, a slayer of a Brahmin. He should dwell among cattle-pens, or indeed in villages or cities.
In penance groves, at sacred fords, or by rivers and springs—
having gone to these places and to the ocean, he shall proclaim his sin and [attain] merit.
Ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length,
it was constructed by Nala under the instructions of Rāmacandra.
Having seen the bridge of the ocean, one casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having seen the bridge, one whose soul is purified may plunge into the sea.
Or rather, a king who is the lord of the earth should perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) when he returns home and approaches for the purpose of dwelling there.
Together with his sons and servants, he should provide a feast for the Brāhmaṇas;
and he should give one hundred cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for those of the four classes.
But through the grace of the Brahmins, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated.
Having killed a woman engaged in a Soma sacrifice, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin.
A twice-born man who is a drinker of intoxicants should go to a river that flows to the ocean;
then, having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, he should provide a meal for Brahmins.
One should give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmins;
having drunk liquor even once, one should drink liquor that is red-hot like fire.
Having himself stolen the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall then torment both himself in this world and in the next.
Taking up a pestle, he should go into the presence of the king for execution;
then, having been released by the king, he attains purification.
But that which is done intentionally deserves a different form of punishment than death;
[the penalty for intentional acts] applies to sitting together, sleeping together, traveling together, conversing together, and eating together.
For sins indeed pass away like a drop of oil upon water;
[the remedies for them are] the Cāndrāyaṇa, the barley-meal fast (yāvaka), and the Tulāpuruṣa.
Following after cows indeed destroys all sins. This is the treatise of Parāśara, consisting of five hundred ślokas [plus] ninety-two;
it is a compendium of the Dharmaśāstra.
Just as the ritual acts of Vedic study [are to be performed], so too is this Dharmaśāstra;
it should be studied with diligent effort by one who is intent on attaining heaven. [No Sūtra on Vyavahāra (only Parāśaramādhava)]...
